analogy.p: Picture a long row of lockers, each holding exactly one letter and each labelled with a number that **starts at 0**. The **length** is how many lockers there are; **substring(start, count)** means 'go to locker number start and read count lockers in a row'; **left** and **right** read from either end; **concatenation** bolts two rows of lockers together end to end. ASC is the secret number written on each letter's tile and CHR looks up the tile that has a given number, so shifting a letter is just moving to the tile with the next number. It breaks down because real lockers can be emptied and refilled in place, whereas operations on strings give a new string and leave the original unchanged unless you assign it back.
analogy.t: A string as a row of lockers

bullets: The five manipulation skills named in the J277 specification are **length**, **substring** (including left and right), **concatenation**, **case conversion** and **ASCII conversion** (ASC and CHR).
Strings are processed one **character** at a time, and each character sits at a numbered **position** (index). The first character is at position **0**.
These operations do not change the original string unless you assign the result back to a variable: word = word.upper changes word, but word.upper on its own just produces a value.

Typical exam contexts: validation (checking length or the first character), data processing (building IDs, initials, email addresses), searching and counting letters, simple encryption (Caesar cipher), and tracing code to give the output.
Link to other topics: data types (2.2), character sets ASCII and Unicode (2.6), validation (2.3), loops (2.2 iteration) and file handling.
core.p: A **string** is a sequence of characters, and **string manipulation** means using built-in operations to examine, cut up, join or change those characters. Programs do this constantly: creating a username from a name, checking the first letter of a postcode, converting text to capitals so a comparison is not case-sensitive, or turning each letter into its character code to encrypt a message. In the OCR reference language the operations are written with a dot after the string name (for example word.length), which is how you will see them in exam papers, and you can use equivalent Python in your own code.

bullets: Example: in word = "Computer", C is at position 0, o is 1, m is 2, p is 3, u is 4, t is 5, e is 6 and r is 7.
The **length** is 8, but the **last position** is 7 (length - 1).
A loop that visits every character must run from 0 to word.length - 1.
Counting from 0 is used throughout programming (arrays, lists) because positions measure the **offset from the start**.
Python also allows negative positions (word[-1] is the last character), but the OCR reference language does not use them, so avoid them in answers marked against the OCR language.
When an exam question says 'starting at position 2', that means the third character.
Link to other topics: arrays (2.2) also start at index 0.
core.h: Positions and indexing: why it starts at 0
core.p: Every character in a string has a position, and in the OCR reference language and in Python the **first character is at position 0**, not 1. This is called **zero-based indexing**. For a string of length n the positions run from 0 to **n - 1**. Getting this wrong is the most common cause of **off-by-one errors**, and trying to read a position that does not exist (for example position 8 in an 8-character string) gives a runtime error.

bullets: OCR: word = "Computer Science" then print(word.length) outputs 16 (8 + 1 space + 7 letters = 16).
Python equivalent: len(word).
Spaces and punctuation count: "Hi there!" has length 9.
The length of an **empty string** "" is 0.
Length gives a loop limit: for i = 0 to word.length - 1 visits every character exactly once.
Length checks in validation: a password must have at least 8 characters, so reject if password.length < 8.
The last character is at position word.length - 1, and word.substring(word.length - 1, 1) returns it.
Length returns an **integer**, so it can be used in arithmetic and comparisons.
core.p: The **length** of a string is the **number of characters** it contains, counted from 1, including spaces, digits and punctuation. In the OCR reference language you write stringname.length (no brackets), and in Python you write len(stringname). Length is used to build loops that process each character, to validate input (a **length check**), and to find the last character.

bullets: OCR example: someText = "Computer Science" then someText.substring(3,3) returns "put" (start at position 3 which is 'p', take 3 characters).
Take one character: word.substring(i, 1) returns the letter at position i.
Python uses slicing with a start and an **end** position (end not included): word[3:6] gives "put". The OCR version uses a start and a **count** - do not mix them up.
If the substring runs past the end of the string, it is an error or returns less than expected, so keep start + count within the length.
Taking the first character: word.substring(0,1); the last character: word.substring(word.length - 1, 1).
Substring can be used to find initials, check a prefix such as a postcode area, and to split a date such as "21/10/2026" (day = date.substring(0,2)).
Substring returns a **string**, even if the characters are digits, so cast to int() if you need to calculate with it.
Exam tip: write out the characters and their positions (0, 1, 2...) before working out a substring.
core.p: A **substring** is a part of a string. In the OCR reference language you extract it with stringname.substring(startingPosition, numberOfCharacters). The first argument is the position to start from (counting from 0) and the second is **how many characters** to take. The result is a new string and the original is not changed. Substring is the most flexible operation: with a length of 1 it extracts a **single character**, which is how programs examine text one letter at a time.

bullets: OCR example: someText = "Computer Science" then someText.left(3) returns "Com" and someText.right(3) returns "nce".
left(1) is the first character; right(1) is the last character.
left(n) is the same as substring(0, n).
right(n) is the same as substring(length - n, n): for "Computer", right(3) = substring(8 - 3, 3) = substring(5,3) = "ter".
These are used to build IDs: surname.left(3) + str(age) might give "PAT15".
Asking for more characters than the string contains leads to an error or a shorter result - validate the length first.
Python has no .left and .right; use slicing word[:3] and word[-3:] in Python code, but in exam answers use the OCR notation.
core.p: The **left** and **right** operations are shortcuts for taking characters from the beginning or end of a string. stringname.left(numberOfCharacters) returns that many characters starting from the **left** (the start), and stringname.right(numberOfCharacters) returns that many characters from the **right** (the end). They are easier to use than substring when you want the first or last few characters, for example the first three letters of a surname or the last four digits of a card number.

bullets: "Hello" + "World" gives "HelloWorld"; "Hello" + " " + "World" gives "Hello World".
The + operator behaves differently by data type: with two integers it adds, with two strings it concatenates.
Joining text to a number needs a **cast**: print("Score: " + str(score)). Without str(), it is a type error.
Building a result: result = "" then result = result + letter in a loop collects letters one at a time.
Order matters: "AB" + "CD" is "ABCD" but "CD" + "AB" is "CDAB".
Concatenation does not change the original strings; it produces a new string that you must assign to a variable or print.
Example: username = forename.left(1) + surname gives "JSmith" for Jane Smith; adding .lower to the whole result would make all usernames consistent.
Link to other topics: casting (2.2 data types), writing output.
core.p: **Concatenation** means joining two or more strings end to end to make a longer string. The operator is **+**. The strings are joined exactly as they are, so you must add any spaces yourself. Concatenation is used for building messages, usernames and file names, and for building up a string inside a loop, for example when reversing a word.

bullets: OCR: someText = "Computer Science" then someText.upper gives "COMPUTER SCIENCE" and someText.lower gives "computer science".
The standard technique for a **case-insensitive comparison**: convert the input first, e.g. if answer.upper == "YES" then ... accepts yes, Yes and YES.
Use it when comparing passwords or usernames that should not depend on case, when sorting names, and when creating consistent IDs.
Case conversion only affects letters: "Pa55word!".upper gives "PA55WORD!".
Remember to **assign** the result if you want to keep it: name = name.lower.
ASCII reason: the capital letter and lower-case letter are 32 apart (A = 65, a = 97), so they are different values to the computer.
To capitalise only the first letter: word.left(1).upper + word.right(word.length - 1).lower.
Link to other topics: validation and authentication (2.3), ASCII (2.6).
core.p: **Case conversion** changes letters from upper case (capitals) to lower case or the other way round. In the OCR reference language stringname.upper converts every letter to upper case and stringname.lower converts every letter to lower case; Python uses .upper() and .lower(). Characters that are not letters (digits, spaces, punctuation) are unchanged. Case conversion is important because computers treat 'A' and 'a' as **different characters** with different codes, so a comparison such as answer == "yes" fails if the user typed "Yes" or "YES".

bullets: ASC("A") returns 65 and CHR(65) returns "A"; ASC("a") returns 97 and CHR(97) returns "a".
Key ASCII values: space = 32, digits '0' to '9' = 48 to 57, capitals 'A' to 'Z' = 65 to 90, lower case 'a' to 'z' = 97 to 122.
Letters are in **alphabetical order** in the code, so CHR(ASC("A") + 1) gives "B": adding 1 moves to the next letter.
A lower-case letter has a code **32 higher** than the matching capital, so ASC("a") - ASC("A") = 32.
The digit character "7" has code 55, which is **not** the number 7 (to get the number, cast it with int("7")).
Characters can be compared because their codes can be compared: "B" > "A" is True (66 > 65).
Standard ASCII uses 7 bits (128 characters); extended ASCII uses 8 bits (256); Unicode uses more bits to represent characters from all languages.
In Python the equivalents are ord("A") (gives 65) and chr(65) (gives "A").
core.p: Every character is stored in the computer as a number from a **character set** such as **ASCII** or **Unicode**. The OCR reference language gives two functions to convert between them. **ASC(character)** returns the **character code** (a whole number) for a character, and **CHR(number)** returns the **character** that has a given code. They let a program do arithmetic on letters, which is the basis of simple encryption and of checking whether a character is a letter or digit.

bullets: Pattern: for i = 0 to word.length - 1 then letter = word.substring(i,1) then (use letter) then next i.
**Counting a letter**: set count = 0, then inside the loop if letter == "e" then count = count + 1.
**Reversing**: set result = "", then loop i from word.length - 1 down to 0 (step -1) adding letter to the end of result, or loop forwards and write result = letter + result.
**Palindrome check**: a word is a palindrome if it equals its reverse ("level", "racecar"), so reverse it then compare, ideally using .lower first.
**Counting vowels**: test whether letter is "a", "e", "i", "o" or "u" using OR conditions, after converting to lower case so that capitals are also counted.
Use .length in the loop limit rather than a fixed number, so the code works for any string.
Do not forget to initialise the result string as "" and the counter as 0 before the loop.
Link to other topics: iteration (2.1/2.2), searching and sorting (2.1), testing (2.3).
core.h: Processing a string one character at a time
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to write or trace a loop that goes through every character of a string. The pattern is always the same: use a **for loop** from 0 to length - 1, pull out each letter with substring(i, 1), do something with it, and (if building a new string) concatenate onto a result variable that starts as an empty string. Mastering this pattern lets you answer reversing, counting, searching and encrypting questions.

bullets: Step 1: read the word and set result = "".
Step 2: for each position i from 0 to word.length - 1, take letter = word.substring(i, 1).
Step 3: code = ASC(letter) + shift, then newLetter = CHR(code).
Step 4: concatenate: result = result + newLetter. After the loop, print(result).
Example: shift 1 turns "HAL" into "IBM" because H (72) becomes 73 = I, A (65) becomes 66 = B and L (76) becomes 77 = M.
Limitation: letters at the end of the alphabet fall off the end: Z (90) + 1 = 91 which is "[". A complete cipher needs wrap-around, for example subtracting 26 when the code is above 90.
To decrypt, use ASC(letter) - shift. The same loop structure applies.
Caesar cipher is weak because there are only 25 possible shifts and the letter frequencies remain, so it is easy to break by trying every shift.
core.h: Using ASC and CHR for a Caesar cipher
core.p: A **Caesar cipher** is a simple form of encryption where every letter is moved a fixed number of places along the alphabet (the **shift**). Because ASC and CHR let you do arithmetic on character codes, a loop can encrypt a message: for each letter, find its code, add the shift, then convert back with CHR. Decrypting does the reverse by subtracting the shift. This is a classic OCR programming question and combines length, substring, concatenation, ASC and CHR.

bullets: Length check: if password.length >= 8 then accept.
Presence check: if name.length > 0 or name != "" then the field is not empty.
Format check example: a code must start with a capital letter A to Z - check ASC(code.left(1)) >= 65 AND ASC(code.left(1)) <= 90.
Case-insensitive check of a command: if choice.lower == "quit" then stop.
Username creation: surname.left(3) + str(birthYear) is a simple rule that must be validated to be unique.
Authentication compares the entered string with a stored one; ask for the **password again** or lock the account after several failed attempts.
Range checks usually apply to numbers, so cast to int first, but length checks are for strings.
Link to other topics: defensive design (2.3), testing (2.3).
core.p: String manipulation is used in defensive design to **validate** what the user types. Because input() returns a string, a program uses string operations to check it meets the rules before using it. A **length check** uses .length, a **presence check** tests the string is not "" (length > 0), and a **format check** looks at specific characters, such as whether the first letters of a code are capitals or the string contains an "@" sign.

bullets: Counting from 1: word.substring(1,1) is the **second** letter, not the first.
Off-by-one in loops: using for i = 0 to word.length goes one past the end and causes a runtime error; use word.length - 1.
Joining a number and a string without str(): "Age " + 15 is a type error.
Forgetting to assign: word.upper on its own does not change word.
Confusing Python slicing (end position excluded) with OCR substring (count of characters).
Mixing up ASC and CHR: ASC("A") is 65 (character to number), CHR(65) is "A" (number to character).
Assuming the digit character "5" equals the number 5: ASC("5") is 53.
Not initialising the result string with "" before concatenating inside a loop.
Link to other topics: types of error (2.3) - these are usually runtime or logic errors.
core.h: Common errors and how to avoid them
core.p: Most marks lost on string questions are because of positions and types. The key habits are: write out the positions from 0, remember that substring uses **start and count**, remember that the last position is **length - 1**, cast before joining numbers and strings, and assign results back to variables. When tracing, copy the string out letter by letter and number the positions underneath.

exam: Always write the string with its positions numbered from 0 underneath before answering any substring, left, right or loop question; it makes slips easy to spot.
'State the output' (1-2 marks): give the exact string result including the case, e.g. "Prog" not Prog if quotation marks are shown in the question.
1-mark definitions: concatenation = joining strings together; length = number of characters; ASC = converts a character to its character code.
Use OCR reference-language notation (.length, .substring, .left, .right, .upper, .lower, ASC, CHR) when writing code, although Python equivalents are accepted if they work; be consistent.

Program-writing questions (4-8 marks) are marked on: taking the input, correct use of the string function, a loop with the correct limits (0 to length - 1), concatenation into a result initialised to "", and output.
'Explain why .upper is used' (2 marks): so the comparison is not case-sensitive (1) because 'a' and 'A' have different character codes (1).
Caesar cipher questions: you need ASC to get the code, add the shift, CHR to convert back, and concatenation to build the result; mention wrap-around for 6-mark answers.
Trace tables for loops over a string: have one column for i, one for letter and one for result; update result row by row.
Casting: any time a number is joined to text, write str(); any time a substring of digits is used in a calculation, write int().
Validation answers: name the check (length check, presence check, format check) and say how it is done with string operations.
State the data type: .length returns an integer; .substring, .left, .right, .upper, .lower and concatenation return strings; ASC returns an integer; CHR returns a character.

mistakes.r: Positions start at 0, so the first character is at position 0 and the last is at length - 1.
mistakes.w: The first character is at position 1.

mistakes.r: The second value is the number of characters to take, so it returns 3 characters starting at position 3 ("put" for Computer Science).
The number must be cast: "Score: " + str(5); otherwise there is a type error.
The result must be assigned: word = word.upper, or used directly in a comparison.
ASC gives the integer code 65; CHR(65) gives the character "A".
mistakes.w: ASC("A") gives "65" as text / CHR(65) gives 65.

mistakes.r: It runs one step too far and causes an error; use word.length - 1.
mistakes.w: A loop for i = 0 to word.length visits every character.

mistakes.r: Spaces and punctuation are characters and are counted in the length.
It is a character with ASCII code 55; use int("7") to get the number 7.
Capitals (65-90) have lower codes than lower-case letters (97-122), so "Z" < "a".
mistakes.w: Lower case comes before capitals in ASCII.

summary: OCR J277 section 2.2 expects you to be able to manipulate strings using the OCR reference-language operations: find the **length**, extract part of a string with **.substring**, **.left** and **.right**, join strings by **concatenation**, change case with **.upper** and **.lower**, and convert between characters and their character codes with **ASC()** and **CHR()**. These skills are used to write and trace short programs on Paper 2 (for example making usernames, checking input, reversing text and encrypting messages), so you must know exactly what each operation returns and that positions start at 0.

terms.d: A sequence of characters (letters, digits, spaces, symbols) treated as one piece of data.
The number of characters in a string, counted from 1, including spaces; written .length in the OCR reference language.
The number showing where a character is in a string; the first character is at position 0.
A part of a string, extracted with .substring(startingPosition, numberOfCharacters).
The .left(n) operation, which returns the first n characters of a string.
The .right(n) operation, which returns the last n characters of a string.
Joining strings together end to end using the + operator.
Changing letters to upper case (.upper) or lower case (.lower).
Function that returns the character code (a whole number) of a character, e.g. ASC("A") = 65.
Function that returns the character that has a given character code, e.g. CHR(65) = "A".
A character set that gives each character a 7-bit binary code, so 'A' is 65 and 'a' is 97.
A character set using more bits per character, able to represent characters from all the world's languages.
A string with no characters in it, written "", whose length is 0.
Repeating a block of code, for example a for loop that visits each character of a string.
A simple encryption that shifts every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet.
Converting a value from one data type to another, e.g. str(5) turns the integer 5 into the string "5".

worked.q: word = "Programming". State the value of (a) word.length (b) word.substring(3,4) (c) word.left(4) (d) word.right(4) (e) word.upper. [5 marks]
steps: Write out positions: P0 r1 o2 g3 r4 a5 m6 m7 i8 n9 g10.
(b) Start at position 3 (g) and take 4 characters: g, r, a, m.
(c) First 4 characters: P, r, o, g.
(d) Last 4 characters: m, i, n, g.

worked.ans:
forename = input("Enter forename")
surname = input("Enter surname")
part = surname.left(3)
part = part.upper
username = part + str(forename.length)
print(username)
For Amelia Patel: part = "PAT", forename.length = 6, so username = "PAT6".
worked.q: Write an algorithm that asks for a forename and a surname and creates a username made of the first 3 letters of the surname in capitals followed by the number of letters in the forename. For Amelia Patel the username is PAT6. [4 marks]
steps: Take the first 3 letters of the surname using .left(3).
Get the length of the forename, cast it to a string and join the parts.

worked.ans:
word = input("Enter word")
result = ""
for i = 0 to word.length - 1
  letter = word.substring(i,1)
  code = ASC(letter) + 1
  result = result + CHR(code)
next i
print(result)
Output for CAT is DBU.
worked.q: Write an algorithm that encrypts a word by changing each letter to the next character in the ASCII table. Show the result for "CAT". [6 marks]
steps: Input the word and set result to an empty string.
Use ASC to get its code, add 1 and convert back with CHR.
Concatenate onto result, then output after the loop.
